title: Design exercise: chat and presence
summary: A classic design exercise: real-time messaging with groups, history, receipts and presence at millions of concurrent connections. The reference answer separates connection gateways from conversation ownership, orders each conversation through a single owner chosen by consistent hashing, partitions history by conversation and time bucket, batches fan-out per gateway, keeps presence best effort and off the message path, and then takes the design down to AWS: one service per box, the message store, event log and compute forks priced at this design's numbers, and a review against the six Well-Architected pillars.

exercise.prompt: Design a messaging service: one-to-one and group conversations, delivered in real time to connected devices, with history that users can scroll back through, delivery and read receipts, and a presence indicator that shows who is online.

constraints.caption: Constraints and numbers.
rows: Send a message to a conversation (up to 1,000 members, assumption); deliver it to every connected member in order; store history forever; page through history.
Delivered and read receipts; online, away and offline presence.
50 million daily active users; 5 million concurrent connections at peak; 1 billion messages per day.
An average message of 200 bytes of text, about 500 bytes stored with metadata; a user reads about 20 messages for every one sent.
derive the per-second rates, the connection count per gateway and the storage growth yourself
Delivery to a connected member within 500 ms at p99 inside one region; history page under 100 ms at p99.
99.95 percent availability for sending and delivery; messages are never lost once the sender sees the acknowledgement.
End-to-end encryption, voice and video, media storage (a media reference is a URL to an object store), spam and abuse detection, search ranking.

clarifying_questions.a: A total order per conversation: every member sees the same sequence. No ordering across conversations.
At least once to the device, deduplicated by message id on the client; the server acknowledges to the sender only after the message is durable.
Up to 1,000 members. Larger broadcast channels are a different product and out of scope.
Yes: a user may have several sessions; each gets every message, and read receipts are per user, not per device.

Online within a few seconds of connecting; offline within 60 s of the last heartbeat (assumption); away is reported by the client when the user is idle, not inferred from heartbeats. Presence is best effort and never blocks a message.
One region per user's home; cross-region conversations route through the conversation's home region. The reference answer is single-region.

blocks.text: Two of these numbers decide the shape of the design. The storage growth says history must be partitioned from day one, and partitioned so that a page of recent messages is one bounded read. The delivery rate says fan-out must be batched: a message to a thousand members cannot cost a thousand network sends.

Clients hold one WebSocket (RFC 6455: upgrade handshake, framing, ping and pong, close) to a stateless-enough gateway that knows only which sessions it holds. Conversations are owned by conversation servers chosen by consistent hashing of the conversation id, so one server orders all writes of a conversation. The conversation server persists the message, assigns its position, and fans it out to the gateways that hold the members' sessions. Offline members get a push notification from an event consumer; a search indexer consumes the same events.

blocks.text: Slack's public write-up describes the same split: gateway servers hold the connections, channel servers are stateful and in memory and each one is mapped to a subset of channels by consistent hashing, and presence servers stand beside them. This answer keeps that shape and adds the bucketed message store that Discord's write-ups describe.

blocks.title: The partition layout: why the bucket exists
items: The partition key is (conversation_id, bucket) with a time-ordered message id as the clustering key, so a page of recent history is a range scan inside one partition.
Discord's public write-up chose a bucket of about 10 days so that even the busiest conversations keep a partition under about 100 MB.
Without the bucket, a years-old conversation becomes one unbounded hot partition, which is the failure Discord's write-up describes.

reference_answer.title: The core flow, step by step

blocks.text: Sending one message to a group, from the sender's frame to the members' screens.

blocks.title: Send, order, persist, fan out, deliver, resync
items: The sender's gateway receives the send frame, checks membership (cached), and forwards it to the conversation server that owns the conversation (consistent hash lookup).

The conversation server assigns the next time-ordered message id (it is the single writer for this conversation, so ids are monotonic within it), writes the message to the store with quorum durability, and only then acknowledges to the sender's gateway. The client's client_msg_id makes a retried send idempotent.

The conversation server looks up the members' sessions in the session registry, groups them by gateway, and sends one batched delivery per gateway (Discord's Elixir write-up describes grouping recipients by node so a publish costs one send per node, not one per recipient).
Each gateway writes the message frame to its local sessions; a client acknowledges delivery, and the gateway updates last_delivered_id for that user asynchronously.
Members without a session are handed to the push notification consumer through the message event log; the message is already durable, so a slow push never blocks delivery.

A reconnecting client sends its last seen message id per conversation; the gateway serves the gap from the store (a range scan in the current bucket) before resuming live delivery, which is how at-least-once delivery survives a dropped connection.

blocks.text: The bottleneck is fan-out in large groups and the hot partition behind a busy conversation. The store sees one write per message regardless of members, but the reads of a popular conversation all land on one partition.

blocks.title: Fan-out in a 1,000-member group
items: One message is up to 1,000 deliveries.
The members' sessions sit on at most 150 gateways, so batching by gateway turns the 1,000 deliveries into at most 150 sends.
Each gateway then writes the frame to its own sessions locally, which costs no network round trip.

blocks.text: Discord's trillions-of-messages write-up reports that hot partitions were their main source of latency, and that a data service layer with request coalescing (one database read for many identical concurrent requests, routed by conversation id with consistent hashing) was the fix, alongside the database move that took their historical-message p99 from 40 to 125 ms down to 15 ms. The answer adopts coalescing in the conversation server: it already owns the conversation, so it serves recent history from an in-memory tail of the last few hundred messages and hits the store only on a miss.

Presence is the other volume problem: a user with 500 contacts coming online would notify 500 sessions, and heartbeats arrive at 170,000 per second. The design keeps presence best effort: status lives in a TTL store written by the gateway on connect, disconnect and every heartbeat; changes are fanned out only to contacts who are currently viewing that user (subscriptions held by the gateway), and status transitions are debounced so a flapping connection does not storm.

blocks.text: The AWS table says what the neutral one could not: the message store is more than two thirds of the bill at both scales, so the storage class and the age at which a bucket leaves the hot store are the levers, and the gateway fleet is the next line, which is why backpressure and connection density per task are tuned before anything else.

L1: Connection gateways separate from conversation ownership, with a message store partitioned by conversation.
Durable write before the acknowledgement, idempotent sends by client message id, and delivery receipts as a cursor per member.
The storage estimate (500 GB per day) and the gateway count derived from the stated assumptions.
L2: Group fan-out batched by gateway, and the hot-partition problem handled with time buckets and request coalescing.
Ordering per conversation by a single owner, with the failover behaviour stated.
History paging by range scan inside a bucket, and the reconnect resync from the last seen message id.
Presence as best effort with TTL, subscriptions and debounce, never on the message path.
L3: Multi-region sessions with a home region per conversation and the latency that costs.
The consequences of end-to-end encryption for search and server-side features.
Explicit backpressure to slow clients, and the cell layout that bounds a store outage.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: ordering, delivery guarantee, group size, multi-device, presence freshness, regions. Say the numbers aloud: 35,000 messages per second at peak, 175,000 deliveries per second, 5 million connections on about 100 gateways, 500 GB of history per day.
0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: Conversation, Message with the (conversation, bucket) partition key, Receipt as a cursor, Session, Presence; the send and ack frames; the history endpoint.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: gateways hold connections, conversation servers hold order by consistent hashing, the store is partitioned by conversation and time bucket, push and search consume an event log.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: the send path (durable write before ack, single-owner ordering, batched fan-out per gateway, resync on reconnect), then hot conversations and presence (bucketed partitions, in-memory tail with coalescing, best-effort presence with subscriptions).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x plan (regions, cells, storage tiers, backpressure), and the L3 sentence: the hard part is not sending a message, it is deciding who owns the order and what happens to that owner when it dies.
Context and scope: The current client platforms, the existing push and identity services, the ordering and loss incidents that motivate the design.
Goals and non-goals: Total order per conversation, no loss after ack, 500 ms delivery p99, 100 ms history p99; encryption, media, voice and abuse detection out of scope.
Design: This answer fills it: the gateway and conversation server split, the partition layout, the send path, presence.
Alternatives considered: Order by store clock or by a consensus log per conversation, long polling instead of WebSocket, receipts per message, with the trade-off table.

Cross-cutting concerns: Observability (delivery latency per hop, fan-out batch size, hot-partition read latency, reconnect rate), privacy of message bodies and retention, cost per connection and per stored message, rollout by conversation cohort.
Review questions the doc must answer: What a member sees in the seconds after a conversation server dies, and how a client proves it has not missed a message after a reconnect.
